about: Hand-picked cases with official records or serious investigations behind them. Kept up to date by the monthly review (see Readme.md). status: unexplained = the investigating body found no explanation; disputed = an explanation exists but is contested or only covers part of the events; explained = the official explanation is broadly accepted.

cases.title: Kenneth Arnold's 'flying saucers'
cases.verdict: No settled explanation; mirages, birds and meteor fragments have been proposed.
cases.summary: A private pilot reported nine bright objects flying in a chain at very high speed past Mount Rainier. His description of them moving 'like a saucer skipped across water' gave the press the phrase 'flying saucer'.
cases.why: The sighting that started the modern UFO era.

cases.title: Roswell debris
cases.verdict: US Air Force reports (1994, 1997): debris from Project Mogul, a classified high-altitude balloon programme.
cases.summary: Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a 'flying disc', then the next day said it was a weather balloon. Interest revived from the late 1970s with claims of a crashed craft and bodies.
cases.why: The most famous UFO case, and an example of a mystery fed by a cover story for a real secret project.

cases.title: Washington radar sightings
cases.verdict: US Air Force (press conference of 29 July 1952): radar echoes caused by temperature inversions.
cases.summary: On two weekends in July 1952, air traffic controllers tracked unknown radar returns over the capital, some also seen as lights by pilots. Jet fighters were sent up without result.
cases.why: Made headlines worldwide and led to the CIA's Robertson Panel in 1953.

cases.title: Valensole landing
cases.verdict: GEIPAN class D: unexplained after investigation.
cases.summary: At dawn a farmer in his lavender field saw a dark craft on the ground and two small figures who quickly got back in before it took off. He found marks in the soil where it had stood; the gendarmerie investigated.
cases.why: One of the best-known French close encounters, still classed as unexplained by GEIPAN.

cases.title: Tehran F-4 intercept
cases.verdict: No official explanation; a US Defense Intelligence Agency report called it 'an outstanding report'. Sceptics point to Jupiter and equipment failures.
cases.summary: After calls about a bright light over the city, two Iranian Air Force F-4 Phantoms were sent up shortly after midnight. Both crews reported losing instruments and communications as they approached it.
cases.why: A military intercept documented in a declassified US intelligence report.

cases.title: Rendlesham Forest
cases.verdict: UK Ministry of Defence: 'of no defence significance'. Sceptics: the Orford Ness lighthouse, a bright meteor and police car lights.
cases.summary: Over several nights, US Air Force personnel from RAF Woodbridge reported lights and a craft in the forest. Deputy base commander Charles Halt sent a memo to the Ministry of Defence; the MoD's file was released through The National Archives.
cases.why: Britain's most famous case, with an official memo from a senior officer.

cases.title: Trans-en-Provence landing traces
cases.verdict: GEIPAN class D: unexplained after investigation.
cases.summary: A man working on his terrace saw a grey, circular craft about 2.5 m wide land a few dozen metres away and leave after a few seconds. GEPAN, GEIPAN's predecessor, had the soil and plants at the site analysed in laboratories.
cases.why: The case with the most extensive physical analysis in GEIPAN's files.

cases.title: Hessdalen lights
cases.verdict: A natural phenomenon still under scientific study; its cause is unknown.
cases.summary: Since late 1981, lights have been seen over this valley, sometimes several times a week in the early years. Project Hessdalen has monitored them with cameras and instruments since 1983, with an automatic station since 1998.
cases.why: A rare recurring phenomenon studied by scientists over decades.

cases.title: Japan Air Lines flight 1628
cases.verdict: The FAA found the crew credible but could not confirm the radar contacts; sceptics suggest Jupiter and Mars.
cases.summary: The crew of a Boeing 747 cargo flight from Paris to Tokyo reported large lights accompanying their aircraft for about 50 minutes over Alaska. The FAA investigated and released its file in 1987.
cases.why: A long sighting by an airline crew, investigated by the FAA.

cases.title: Belgian wave
cases.verdict: The famous triangle photo (Petit-Rechain, April 1990) was a hoax, admitted in 2011; the radar returns of 30–31 March 1990 remain debated.
cases.summary: From November 1989 to 1991, thousands of people reported large triangles with lights. On the night of 30–31 March 1990 the Belgian Air Force scrambled two F-16s after radar detections; the pilots saw nothing.
cases.why: One of the largest waves of sightings, with an air force that made its data public.

cases.title: Air France flight AF3532
cases.verdict: GEIPAN class D: unexplained after investigation.
cases.summary: The crew of an Air France A320 from Nice to London saw a large dark brown or red disc change shape and vanish. At the same moment a military radar recorded an unidentified track for 50 seconds crossing the flight's path.
cases.why: An airline crew's sighting matched by a military radar record.

cases.title: Phoenix Lights
cases.verdict: US Air Force: flares dropped by A-10 aircraft on a training exercise; the earlier V of lights was a formation of A-10s. Some witnesses reject this.
cases.summary: Thousands of people across Arizona saw a V of lights pass overhead, and later a row of stationary lights near Phoenix. The evening was widely filmed.
cases.why: One of the most widely witnessed sightings, and a lesson in how two events can merge into one story.

cases.title: USS Nimitz 'Tic Tac'
cases.verdict: The Pentagon released the infrared video in April 2020; the object remains unidentified.
cases.summary: During exercises of the USS Nimitz carrier group, Navy pilots were sent to check radar contacts and described a white, wingless object shaped like a Tic Tac. A later crew filmed it with an infrared camera.
cases.why: The case that, with the 2017 New York Times article, brought UAPs back into US politics.

cases.title: Mirage patrol over Nancy
cases.verdict: GEIPAN class D: unexplained after investigation.
cases.summary: A Mirage pilot reported being 'followed' by an aircraft behind his patrol. The leader also saw a dot that disappeared after 15 to 20 seconds, but ground controllers found no trace of other traffic.
cases.why: A brief encounter reported by military pilots, unexplained by GEIPAN.

cases.title: O'Hare airport disc
cases.verdict: The FAA did not investigate and called it a probable weather phenomenon; no photo or radar record has been confirmed.
cases.summary: United Airlines staff and pilots reported a dark grey disc hovering over gate C17 before shooting up through the clouds and leaving a hole in them.
cases.why: Seen by aviation professionals at one of the busiest airports in the world.
